title: SYSK Selects: Your limb is torn off - now what?
summary: SYSK Selects rerun, chosen by Josh, of the episode "So your limb's torn off. Now what?" The hosts cover the 1962 case of Eddie Everett Knowles Jr., a boy whose arm was torn off by a train near Somerville, Massachusetts, and who became the first human to have a full limb reattached at Mass General. They explain the history and steps of microsurgery and replantation, first-aid advice for severed limbs (call 911, stop bleeding, keep the part cool on ice but not in direct contact or water), the surgical sequence (arteries and veins, bone, later nerves and skin), toe-to-thumb transfers, free flap transfers, cross transfer leg surgery, and regenerative use of extracellular matrix (pig bladder powder) that helped a Cincinnati hobby shop owner regrow a fingertip and nail bed. The episode closes with a listener correction about the history of syphilis in Europe.

segments.title: Selects introduction
segments.summary: Josh introduces this week's Selects pick, a classic episode about limb reattachment, and the show opens with banter about Jerry being sick.

segments.title: Eddie Knowles and the 1962 train accident
segments.summary: Eddie Everett Knowles Jr. grabbed onto a gravel train near Somerville, Massachusetts, was thrown into a tunnel support and lost his arm. He walked uphill, was helped by workers and a woman who applied pressure, and was taken to Mass General, where surgeons reattached the arm in May 1962, the first successful full human limb reattachment.

segments.title: How the 1962 reattachment was done and microsurgery
segments.summary: Surgeons had reattached arteries, nerves, and bone in animals and parts of humans before but never all at once. The boy's age helped because arteries clot more readily in children. Surgeons restored circulation first, then bone was joined with a screw, and nerves were deferred. Microsurgery under a microscope with very fine suture thread is explained, along with the history of its acceptance, and the mention of dogs in early experiments.

segments.title: Toe-to-thumb transfers and free flap surgery
segments.summary: The hosts discuss toe-to-thumb transfers from the 1960s, which restore hand function, and free flap tissue transfers from the 1970s, where tissue is harvested from another body area and reattached with microsurgery as a skin graft. They also describe a case where fingers were inserted under the skin of an arm to grow new skin.

segments.title: First aid and what to do after a limb is severed
segments.summary: Advice: call 911, stop bleeding with pressure or a tourniquet, place the severed part in a sealed bag, then pack it on ice without direct contact with ice or water, since water and ice can cause damage such as frostbite. Hospital surgeons usually reattach bone, then blood vessels, with the timeline being as short as possible; a limb may survive hours at room temperature and up to about four days refrigerated, with muscle degradation the main concern.

segments.title: Cross transfer surgery and rehabilitation
segments.summary: The hosts describe cross transfer surgery, in which a lower leg is turned around and attached to a damaged upper leg so the calf muscles take over thigh function, with a prosthesis. They also mention rehabilitation after reattachment being long and that the reattached limb can feel different.

segments.title: Regrowing fingertips with extracellular matrix
segments.summary: A Cincinnati hobby shop owner whose fingertip was cut off below the nail regrew the finger and nail bed after extracellular matrix, derived from pig bladder powder stripped of cells, was applied to the wound. The hosts explain that extracellular matrix signals the body to regenerate rather than scar, and that mammals lose this ability with age, with research on regrowing limbs ongoing, including trials with war veterans.

segments.title: Listener mail: syphilis correction and sign-off
segments.summary: A listener corrects the earlier statement that Europeans did not know syphilis before the Lewis and Clark expedition, noting it was documented in late fifteenth century Europe. The hosts thank her and sign off with reminders on contacting the show.
